Overview

Kraków as a Business Centre

Kraków, capital of the Malopolska voivodeship, had about 807,600 residents in mid-2024 according to Statistics Poland, and the city estimates that at least a million people live and work there. Its economy is built on knowledge-intensive services. The Association of Business Service Leaders counted 312 business services centres in Kraków employing nearly 108,000 people at the end of the first quarter of 2025, making it one of Poland's main hubs for finance, IT and shared services operations run by international groups. The city reports more than 500 technology businesses employing almost 50,000 IT specialists, 23 universities with about 130,000 students, and an office market of more than 1.8 million square metres.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Kraków largely because of what happens inside its service centres and technology firms. Multinationals running finance, procurement and IT operations in the city face risks of payment fraud, vendor collusion, data theft and conflicts of interest among staff who control processes for operations worldwide. Investors in Kraków start-ups and acquirers of software houses need background research on founders, shareholders and intellectual property claims. Outsourcing and IT contracting relationships generate disputes over performance, staff poaching and misuse of confidential information. Creditors and buyers also follow restructuring and insolvency proceedings before the Kraków courts, which handle cases for much of the Malopolska region.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Kraków

01

Shared services centre fraud

Fact-finding support for counsel and internal audit when a Kraków finance, procurement or payments centre detects irregularities, such as fictitious vendors, manipulated bank details or kickbacks, including research into suppliers and related companies registered in the KRS and links to employees revealed by public records.

02

IT vendor and outsourcing diligence

Background research on Kraków software houses, IT contractors and outsourcing providers before significant contracts, covering KRS ownership and management history, filed financial statements, litigation and insolvency records, and reported disputes over delivery, subcontracting or data security.

03

Start-up and technology investment diligence

Pre-investment research on founders, shareholders and prior ventures of Kraków technology companies, checking corporate history in the KRS, beneficial ownership entries, litigation, insolvency bans and media coverage so investors can test representations made during funding rounds and acquisitions.

04

Departing staff and competing ventures

Lawful research supporting counsel where former managers or engineers of a Kraków centre are suspected of setting up competing businesses, diverting clients or taking confidential information, identifying newly registered companies, their shareholders and officers, and connections to former colleagues.

05

Insolvency and restructuring research

Research for creditors and potential buyers in insolvency and restructuring proceedings before the Kraków courts, covering the debtor's group structure, related parties, pledges recorded in the register of pledges, changes in management before insolvency and any bans on conducting business.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Kraków

Kraków registry and commercial divisions

The District Court for Kraków-Srodmiescie houses two National Court Register divisions: the XI Commercial Division for entities with registered offices in Kraków and the XII Division for the rest of Malopolska. Its IV and V Commercial Divisions hear business-to-business cases from across the Kraków court area, and the VII Division keeps the register of pledges for Malopolska and Swietokrzyskie. Paper registration files predating July 2021 remain with these registry divisions.

Insolvency and restructuring division

The VIII Commercial Division of the District Court for Kraków-Srodmiescie handles bankruptcy and restructuring proceedings, and bans on conducting business, for several district courts in the Kraków area, including Krowodrza, Nowa Huta and Podgorze. Filings in these proceedings are generally made through the National Register of Debtors, which also provides a public source of information about debtors, proceedings and court-appointed administrators.

Higher courts in Kraków

Kraków is also the seat of a regional court, which hears larger commercial cases at first instance and appeals from the district courts, and of a court of appeal for the wider region. Establishing which Kraków court and division has handled a counterparty's disputes is a useful step in reconstructing its litigation and enforcement history, although judgments are not uniformly published online.

The business services ecosystem

Kraków's service centres are largely foreign-owned and operate across finance, IT, procurement and customer operations, supported by a dense office market and a large university population. The Association of Business Service Leaders and the city's own investor services publish annual data on the sector. For investigations, this means evidence and personnel often sit in Kraków while the affected business, data and decision-makers are elsewhere, requiring coordination across jurisdictions.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Kraków

TDSC scopes Kraków matters from Nashville and begins by mapping where the relevant people, data and decisions sit, since a Kraków service centre often serves operations in many countries. Desk research uses the National Court Register, filed financial statements, the Central Register of Beneficial Owners, the register of pledges, the National Register of Debtors and Polish media. Personal data is processed on a documented lawful basis under the GDPR, with particular care for employee data in internal matters. Where information must be gathered in Poland beyond desk research, TDSC coordinates detectives licensed under Polish law and works with the client's Polish counsel. TDSC has no office in Kraków.

TDSC has no office in Kraków. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Kraków: Frequently Asked Questions

Does TDSC have an office in Kraków?

No. TDSC is based in Nashville and has no office, staff or address in Poland. Engagements touching Kraków are scoped and managed from Nashville. Where a matter requires work in the city beyond desk research, TDSC coordinates detectives licensed under Polish law and works alongside the client's Polish counsel.

Where are Kraków companies registered?

Companies with registered offices in Kraków are entered in the National Court Register through the XI Commercial Division of the District Court for Kraków-Srodmiescie, while companies elsewhere in Malopolska are handled by its XII Division. Current KRS data and recent filings are searchable online; older registration files are held on paper at the registry division.

Can TDSC support an internal investigation at a Kraków service centre?

TDSC can support the client's counsel and internal audit with external research on suppliers, related companies and individuals, and with structuring the fact-finding. Processing of employee data must have a lawful basis under the GDPR and respect Polish employment law, so the scope is agreed with Polish counsel before any review of personal data or interviews.

How can insolvency proceedings in Kraków be followed?

Bankruptcy and restructuring proceedings for much of the Kraków area are handled by the VIII Commercial Division of the District Court for Kraków-Srodmiescie, with filings made through the National Register of Debtors. That register and court announcements provide public information on debtors and administrators, which TDSC combines with KRS history and related-party research.

Can TDSC check a Kraków software house before we outsource to it?

Yes. TDSC can review the company's KRS history, shareholders and beneficial owners, management changes, filed accounts, litigation and insolvency records, and published reporting on disputes or data incidents. The research is based on lawful public and commercial sources and is designed to inform contract terms, security requirements and the decision whether to proceed.
